EVERY AGENT IN THE CANONICAL ROSTER MUST APPEAR. A missing agent is not a smaller roster — it is an agent with no identity at the moment the pipeline invokes it, and the run has nowhere else to look. Do not decide that an agent is irrelevant to this project; you cannot know which seams a run will reach. mocka-fare-detective, mockb-schedule-detective, fare-boundary-fixer and stop-rendering-fixer must appear alongside every other canonical agent, each entry naming its true ancestor.

## How to specialise

For each agent, keep WHAT IT DOES and replace WHAT IT KNOWS. The generic persona states a role; your version states that same role against mock-a and mock-b — vitest and typescript, mocka's src/fares.ts and mockb's src/schedule.ts, the age-comparison logic behind MOCK3-1, the departure-board rendering loop behind MOCK3-2, and whatever conventions and commands you find by actually reading those files. Read the code to find these. An assertion about the codeline that you did not verify is worse than a generic sentence, because the next reader cannot tell which is which.

Do not weaken a rule while specialising it. If the generic persona forbids something, says a finding must carry evidence, or names a check that must pass, that survives verbatim in meaning — you are changing what the agent knows, never what it is required to do. In particular: an investigator persona (mocka-fare-detective, mockb-schedule-detective) stays read-only and must not be given license to edit fares.ts or schedule.ts; an implementer persona (fare-boundary-fixer, stop-rendering-fixer) keeps whatever verification-before-claiming-done requirement its ancestor states.

KEEP EACH PERSONA AT THE LENGTH THE WORK NEEDS. A persona that lists every file in the repository is not more specialised, it is less usable: the agent reads it before every invocation.

## Ancestry

Each entry names the canonical agent it derives from. For an agent that exists in the canonical roster, that is the agent itself. mocka-fare-detective and mockb-schedule-detective derive from this project's canonical investigator agent; fare-boundary-fixer and stop-rendering-fixer derive from this project's canonical implementer agent — confirm the exact canonical names against the file at __CANONICAL_COPY_PATH__ rather than assuming them.

If this project needs an agent the canonical roster does not have, you may add one — but it MUST name the canonical agent it is closest to as its ancestor. That is not bookkeeping: an agent inherits its ladder, its tool grant and its output contract from its ancestor, so an agent invented from nothing has no budget, no tools and no way for the pipeline to receive what it returns.

`derivedFromSha256` is the SHA-256 of the ancestor's persona text exactly as it appears in the canonical copy you were given. It records what you derived from, so that a later change to the canonical roster is detectable rather than silent.

## Which seam an agent enters by

An agent does not run on its own. It enters the pipeline through a SEAM, which decides its ladder, its tool grant, its output contract and the prompt it executes. For an agent that exists in the canonical roster, the seam is already known and you do not state it.

For an agent you ADD, name the seam in the `seam` field. It must be one the pipeline already declares — you are choosing which existing door this agent comes through, not inventing one. If none fits, the agent you are adding is doing work the pipeline has no place for, and adding it will not create that place.

Omitting it does not leave the question open: the name is matched against patterns instead, and a pattern is a guess about what an agent does based on how it is spelled. That is how an agent named for review came to enter through an inference seam, with another seam's budget and tools.

## What you are not doing

You are not editing the canonical roster. You are not judging whether an agent should exist. You are not writing prompts — an agent's persona says who it is; its instructions for a task live in that task's prompt.
